results.q: What happens when the output buffer is full while encoding?
answer: When the output buffer is full, `pb_write()` returns an error by calling `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "stream full")`.

This is handled in pb_write() (pb_encode.c:95): it checks `count > 0 && stream->callback != NULL`, and when that is true it checks `stream->bytes_written + count < stream->bytes_written || stream->bytes_written + count > stream->max_size` (line 97); if true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "stream full")`; then it checks `!stream->callback(stream, buf, count)` (line 107); if true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")`; then it calls one of write_callback(), buf_write() through pb_ostream_s.callback — which one depends on the data at run time (line 107).

buf_write() sets `pb_byte_t *dest = (pb_byte_t*)stream->state` (line 55); then it sets `stream->state = dest + count` (line 56); then it checks `buf != NULL` (line 64); if true it calls memcpy(); then it returns `true` (line 69).

results.q: What happens when the decoder needs more bytes than are left in the input?
answer: When the decoder needs more bytes than are left, `pb_read()` checks `stream->bytes_left < count` and, if true, returns `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")`, skipping the rest of its body. Consequently `read_callback()` and `buf_read()` are not executed, leaving the previous values unchanged. The caller `pb_skip_varint()` then sees `!pb_read(stream, &byte, 1)` and returns `false`.

This is handled in pb_read() (pb_decode.c:103): it checks `stream->bytes_left < count`, and when that is true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")`, so the rest of pb_read() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: read_callback(), buf_read() — the previous values stay in place.
pb_read()'s caller pb_skip_varint() checks `!pb_read(stream, &byte, 1)` (pb_decode.c:261) and then returns `false`.

results.q: What happens when a decoded message is missing a required field?
answer: When a decoded message is missing a required field, `pb_decode_inner()` checks `(req_field_count & 31) != 0` and then verifies `fields_seen.bitfield[req_field_count >> 5] != (allbits >> (uint_least8_t)(32 - (req_field_count & 31)))`; if this condition is true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "missing required field")`.

This is handled in pb_decode_inner() (pb_decode.c:1205): it checks `(req_field_count & 31) != 0`, and when that is true it checks `fields_seen.bitfield[req_field_count >> 5] != (allbits >> (uint_least8_t)(32 - (req_field_count & 31)))` (line 1207); if true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "missing required field")`.

results.q: What happens when a varint is too long?
answer: When a varint exceeds the 64‑bit limit, `pb_decode_varint()` checks `bitpos >= 63 && (byte & 0xFE) != 0` and if true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "varint overflow")`. The caller `pb_decode_svarint()` then sees `!pb_decode_varint(stream, &value)` and returns `false`, and its caller `pb_dec_varint()` likewise returns `false`.

This is decided in pb_decode_varint() (pb_decode.c:241): it checks `!pb_readbyte(stream, &byte)`; when that is NOT true it checks `bitpos >= 63 && (byte & 0xFE) != 0` (line 244); if true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "varint overflow")`; then it sets `result |= (uint64_t)(byte & 0x7F) << bitpos` (line 247); then it sets `bitpos = (uint_fast8_t)(bitpos + 7)` (line 248).

results.q: What happens when a field arrives with the wrong wire type?
answer: When a field arrives with the wrong wire type, `decode_basic_field()` detects it and immediately returns an error via `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "wrong wire type")`, skipping the rest of the function. Consequently, the specific decoding functions (`pb_dec_bool()`, `pb_dec_varint()`, `pb_decode_fixed32()`, `pb_decode_fixed64()`) are not executed, so the previous values remain unchanged. Additionally, other parts of the code, such as `pb_message_set_to_defaults()`, reject the bad input when `!decode_field(&defstream, wire_type, iter)`.

Invalid data is caught in decode_basic_field() (pb_decode.c:431): it checks `wire_type != PB_WT_VARINT && wire_type != PB_WT_PACKED`, and when that is true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "wrong wire type")`, so the rest of decode_basic_field() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: pb_dec_bool(), pb_dec_varint(), pb_decode_fixed32(), pb_decode_fixed64() — the previous values stay in place.
Bad input is also rejected in other places: pb_message_set_to_defaults() rejects it when `!decode_field(&defstream, wire_type, iter)` (pb_decode.c:1031).

results.q: What happens when messages are nested too deeply?
answer: When a nested message exceeds the allowed depth, `pb_make_string_substream()` records the size and reduces the parent stream’s `bytes_left`. This causes subsequent `pb_read()` or `pb_readbyte()` calls to see `stream->bytes_left < count` or `stream->bytes_left == 0`, which may return early and skip callbacks. The caller functions (`decode_static_field`, `decode_callback_field`, `pb_decode_ex`, `pb_dec_submessage`) then detect the failure of `pb_make_string_substream()` and return `false`.

This is decided in pb_make_string_substream() (pb_decode.c:393): it checks `substream->bytes_left < size`; when that is NOT true it records it (`substream->bytes_left = (size_t)size`, `stream->bytes_left -= (size_t)size`).
Consequence: pb_read() checks `stream->bytes_left < count` (pb_decode.c:103); `stream->bytes_left < count` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
Consequence: pb_readbyte() checks `stream->bytes_left == 0` (pb_decode.c:126); `stream->bytes_left == 0` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
pb_make_string_substream()'s caller decode_static_field() checks `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (pb_decode.c:519) and then returns `false`.
pb_make_string_substream()'s caller decode_callback_field() checks `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (pb_decode.c:804) and then returns `false`.
pb_make_string_substream()'s caller pb_decode_ex() checks `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (pb_decode.c:1230) and then returns `false`.
pb_make_string_substream()'s caller pb_dec_submessage() checks `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (pb_decode.c:1649) and then returns `false`.

results.q: What happens when an array has more items than its maximum size during encoding?
answer: When an array has more items than its maximum size during encoding, `encode_array()` checks `PB_ATYPE(field->type) != PB_ATYPE_POINTER && count > field->array_size`; if true it returns via `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "array max size exceeded")`, skipping the rest of the function. Consequently, `pb_encode_tag()`, `pb_enc_varint()`, `pb_encode_varint()`, and `pb_write()` are not executed and the previous values remain unchanged.

This is handled in encode_array() (pb_encode.c:150): it checks `PB_ATYPE(field->type) != PB_ATYPE_POINTER && count > field->array_size`, and when that is true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "array max size exceeded")`, so the rest of encode_array() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: pb_encode_tag(), pb_enc_varint(), pb_encode_varint(), pb_write() — the previous values stay in place.

results.q: What happens when the decoder reads a tag of zero?

Because it returns early, the functions `pb_field_iter_find()`, `pb_field_iter_find_extension()`, `decode_extension()`, and `pb_skip_field()` do not run, leaving the previous values unchanged.

Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: pb_field_iter_find(), pb_field_iter_find_extension(), decode_extension(), pb_skip_field() — the previous values stay in place.

It is called by pb_read() at pb_decode.c:93, only when `count == 0` is false, only when `buf == NULL && stream->callback != buf_read` is true, repeatedly inside `while (count > 16)`; pb_read() at pb_decode.c:99, only when `count == 0` is false, only when `buf == NULL && stream->callback != buf_read` is true; pb_skip_varint() at pb_decode.c:261, repeatedly inside `do-while`; pb_skip_string() at pb_decode.c:278, only when `!pb_decode_varint32(stream, &length)` is false, only when `(size_t)length != length` is false. The full chain from the program's start is: main() → listdir() → pb_decode_ex() → pb_close_string_substream() → pb_read().

`pb_ostream_s.bytes_written` is set by `pb_ostream_from_buffer()` (line 86), by `pb_write()` (line 112), and by `pb_encode_submessage()` (lines 768 and 775). It is read by `main()` (line 32), `pb_write()` (line 97), `encode_array()` (line 180), `pb_get_encoded_size()` (line 573), and `pb_encode_submessage()` (line 750). The value flows from `pb_ostream_s.bytes_written` through `pb_encode_submessage()` → `pb_write()` → `write_callback()` → `send()` and ultimately influences the socket send.
pb_ostream_s.bytes_written is a field of type `size_t`, defined in pb_encode.h:51 — the code describes it as: "Number of bytes written so far.".

It is set by pb_ostream_from_buffer() (`stream.bytes_written = 0`, line 86); pb_write() (`stream->bytes_written += count`, line 112); pb_encode_submessage() (`substream.bytes_written = 0`, line 768); pb_encode_submessage() (`stream->bytes_written += substream.bytes_written`, line 775).

Following where its value goes: pb_ostream_s.bytes_written → pb_encode_submessage() → pb_write() → write_callback() → send() — so it ultimately influences send(), which is an output (socket send).
